title: Jātavedase sunavāma: the hymn to Durgā
theme: Seven verses to Agni Jātavedas and the goddess Durgā asking to be carried across every difficulty, as a boat carries across the sea.

Read by the anonymous commentator as a vocative, ‘O you who carry [us] well across’ («हे सुतरसि»); by Bhāskara as a verb, ‘you carry [us] well across’ («त्वमेव सुतरसि सुष्ठु तारयसि»), with tarase as a vocative of the goddess.
Taken by the anonymous commentator as ‘forgiving’ (from √kṣam); Bhāskara instead as ‘what perishes’, from √kṣai («क्षामत् क्षयशीलं वस्त्व्»).

translation.literal: To Jātavedas let us press soma; may the knower burn down those who are hostile. May he carry us across all difficulties; as with a boat across the sea, Agni [carries us] across troubles. To her, fire-coloured, blazing with heat, belonging to the radiant one, favoured in the fruits of action — to Durgā the goddess I go for refuge; you who carry across well, to the one who carries across, homage. O Agni, to be praised, carry us safely across all difficulties; let our fort be broad and abundant, our land wide; be welfare and health for our children and descendants. Destroyer of difficulties, Jātavedas, you carry us across all troubles as across the sea by a boat. O Agni, praised in the mind like Atri, be the protector of our bodies. Let us call Agni, conqueror of armies, overpowering, fierce, from his highest seat; may he carry us across all difficulties, the forgiving god, Agni [carrying us] across troubles. You spread happiness, praised at the sacrifices; of old and new you sit as hotṛ. O Agni, gladden your own body, and bestow good fortune on us. What is enjoyed by cows, poured down, of you the unjoined one, O Indra, of Viṣṇu — may we follow it. Dwelling upon the vault of heaven, may they gladden [me, devoted] to Viṣṇu, here in this world.
translation.readable: For the fire that knows all, let us press the soma; may he burn away all that is hostile, and carry us across every danger, as a boat carries across the sea. In the fire-bright goddess Durgā, blazing with her own heat, I take refuge; homage to her who carries us across. Agni, carry us safely over every hardship; make our home broad and our land wide; be well-being for our children. Watch over us as the sage Atri does; we call you from your highest place, conqueror and protector; forgive our faults and carry us across. Praised at every rite, gladden yourself and give us good fortune. May we follow Indra and Viṣṇu, and may the gods who dwell above give joy here to the one devoted to Viṣṇu.

syntax: Seven triṣṭubh verses, each in two printed lines. The first, second and fifth turn on the verb √pṛ ‘carry across’ (parṣat, pāraya, atiparṣi), with the image of the boat (nāvā iva/na sindhum). The second verse is the act of refuge (śaraṇam ahaṃ prapadye) to Durgā; the others are prayers to Agni, ending with Indra and Viṣṇu.

ambiguities.note: The hymn names the goddess Durgā only in the second verse; the rest address Agni. Bhāskara: Agni is presented as the special fire that is Durgā («अग्निर् अग्रणीर् दुर्गारूपोऽग्निविशेषः प्रतिपाद्यते»); Sāyaṇa: Durgā as known from the Durgā rituals and the mantra-śāstras («येयं नवदुर्गाकल्पादिषु मन्त्रशास्त्रेषु प्रसिद्धा»), which the anonymous commentator repeats.
‘Hard places, dangers’: misfortunes for the anonymous commentator («विश्वा दुर्गाणि सर्वा आपदोऽतिपर्षत्»); places such as saṃsāra for Bhāskara («स्थानानि संसारादीन्य्»).

metre.name: triṣṭubh
metre.note: Seven triṣṭubh verses printed as fourteen half-verses, counted 22, 21, 22, 21, 20, 21, 22, 20, 22, 22, 20, 20, 21 and 22 syllables. The shortfalls come from vowels joined in the print (duritāty agniḥ, nāveva) and from the fourth half-verse (sutarasi tarase namaḥ), whose second pāda has 9 or 10 syllables; the Ṛgveda verses 1.99.1 and 1.189.2 that open verses one and three have the full count.

beginner: This is the hymn many people know as the Durgā Sūkta. Its picture is a crossing: as a boat carries people over the sea, so may the fire-god, Agni, “the one who knows all that is born”, carry us over every danger and every wrong. In the second verse the speaker takes refuge in the goddess Durgā, bright as fire and blazing with her own heat, and greets her as the one who carries across. The other verses ask Agni to burn away what is hostile, to make the home secure and the land wide, to watch over the family, to forgive faults, and to bring good fortune; the last calls on Indra and Viṣṇu. Bhāskara says these verses are used in recitation and offerings when fear or misfortune comes; the anonymous commentator, for warding off harm. The record reports this and claims nothing about what reciting it achieves.
analogy: Like a ferryman asked, in seven different ways, to take passengers safely over a wide and dangerous river.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: In seven verses it presses soma for Jātavedas and asks him to burn the hostile and carry us across all difficulties as a boat crosses the sea; takes refuge in the fire-coloured goddess Durgā; asks Agni to carry us across, make our dwelling broad and be welfare for our children; to protect our bodies; it calls Agni from his highest seat; praises him as the priest of old and new; and asks to follow Indra and Viṣṇu.

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Bhāskara: these Durgā mantras are for japa and homa when fear of thieves, tigers or spirits arises, or in misfortune — «चोरव्याघ्रपिशाचादिभये समुपस्थिते दौर्गत्ये च जपहोमादिकर्म एभिः कुर्यात्». Sāyaṇa and the anonymous commentator: mantras to be recited for warding off harm («अथानिष्टपरिहारार्थत्वेन जप्या मन्त्रा उच्यन्ते», Sāyaṇa), the first verse explained as the ṛk to Agni who burns enemies and carries us across sins as a boatman carries across the sea.

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The anonymous commentator and Sāyaṇa: the Durgā known from the Durgā rituals, called vairocanī because she is seen by Virocana, the supreme self — «विशेषेण रोचते स्वयमेव प्रकाशत इति विरोचनः परमात्मा, तेन दृष्टत्वाद्वैरोचनीम्» (Sāyaṇa). Bhāskara: the supreme nature belonging to the god who shines in many forms («विविधमाविर्भवतः देवस्य स्वभूतां परप्रकृतिं»), and Durgā is a name of fire («दुर्ग इत्यग्नेर्नाम तदात्मिका देवी दुर्गा», in his comment on the Durgā gāyatrī of 10.1).

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Sāyaṇa and the anonymous commentator take Atri as a liberated sage, free of the three afflictions, who wishes all beings well in his mind; Agni is asked to do the same and so protect our bodies. Sāyaṇa quotes two verses for the attitude: «आत्मौपम्येन भूतानां दयां कुर्वीत मानवः» and «सर्वे च सुखिनः सन्तु सर्वे सन्तु निरामयाः».

commentary.q: Where do the verses come from?
commentary.label: linguistic
commentary.text: The first verse is the Ṛgveda’s 1.99.1 and the third its 1.189.2, with small differences of spelling; the others are found elsewhere in the Vedic hymns (see references). The commentators of this text explain all seven; Sāyaṇa and Bhāskara stop before the seventh (gobhir juṣṭam), which only the anonymous commentator explains. The witnesses differ in a few slips and in the reading नावा / वावा in the seventh half-verse, which the sources page lists for review.

schools.disagreement: The commentaries available are ritual and Vedic; none takes a position on which the Vedānta schools named here divide. No Viśiṣṭādvaita or Dvaita commentary on the Mahānārāyaṇa is in the edition’s sources (Raṅgarāmānuja’s is not available here). The commentators differ on whether the hymn is chiefly to Agni with Durgā as his form (Bhāskara) or to Durgā of the Durgā rituals (the anonymous commentator, Sāyaṇa).

parallels.quote: जातवेदसे सुनवाम सोममरातीयतो नि दहाति वेदः
parallels.note: The first verse of the hymn is the single verse of Ṛgveda 1.99.
The third verse is Ṛgveda 1.189.2, with the same unelided navyo asmān.

contemporary.text: The hymn returns again and again to one picture: a crossing, made safely with help. It does not promise that the water will be calm, only that one need not cross alone. This is a modern reflection on the passage, not part of its traditional meaning.

reflect.beginner: Why might a prayer for safety use the image of a boat rather than, say, a wall?
reflect.deeper: The hymn names Durgā once and Agni throughout. What does it mean to take refuge in a goddess within a hymn to fire, and how do the commentators handle it?
reflect.practice: Think of one “crossing” in your life now, and name who or what helps you across it.

references.text: Other verses of the hymn also occur in the Ṛgveda outside its first book (for example the fourth verse, viśvāni no durgahā, at RV 5.4.9); the edition’s Ṛgveda source covers only the first book, so these are noted here and not quoted.
Sāyaṇa and Bhāskara comment on this hymn within their first anuvāka; Bhāskara refers verses three and four to his comments elsewhere in the Āraṇyaka («अग्ने त्वमिति व्याख्याता ‘उभा वां’ इत्यत्र»).

flags.note: In सिन्धुं न नावा the Tirupati e-text reads वावा; the base and the Ānandāśrama text read नावा. Listed for checking.
Whether the hymn is addressed chiefly to Agni with Durgā as his form, or to Durgā, is a matter of commentary.
